# The Slow Argument of Lichen

There is a gravestone somewhere in nearly every old churchyard that has gone quietly gold. The name has become hard to read, and the dates are half-swallowed by crusts of orange, sage, and a grey-green like old copper. Most people who notice this feel a small melancholy about time, erosion, and forgetting. The stone is being reclaimed and the dead are being blurred.

I want to argue for a different feeling. What is happening on that gravestone is one of the strangest and most philosophically unsettling phenomena on the planet, and it has been happening in plain sight for as long as there have been rocks and weather. The gold crust is not decay. It is a partnership so intimate that for most of human history nobody realized it was a partnership at all.

---

Here is the basic fact, which still seems to me like a magic trick: a lichen is not an organism. Or rather, it is an organism in the way a city is an organism, or a marriage, or a conversation. It is built from a fungus and a photosynthetic partner, usually a green alga, sometimes a cyanobacterium, sometimes both. The fungus provides structure, shelter, and a grip on the world. The photosynthesizer provides sugar. Together they make something neither could make alone: a body with its own shape, color, chemistry, and way of living, a body that looks nothing like either of its parents.

That last part is what makes lichens so disorienting. If you grow the fungus of a lichen by itself in a lab, it usually becomes a formless smudge, a sad little colony with none of the elaborate architecture of the wild lichen. The leafy lobes, the tiny cups, the beard-like strands hanging from spruce branches all appear only when the partners come together. The form of the lichen belongs to neither of them. It belongs to the relationship.

For centuries, naturalists classified lichens as plants, then as their own odd category, then as something in between. They had names, Latin binomials, careful descriptions. They were treated as individuals because they looked like individuals. Then, in 1867, a Swiss botanist named Simon Schwendener proposed what came to be called the "dual hypothesis": that lichens were actually fungi living with algae. They were two things, not one.

The reaction was not gratitude. Many of the leading lichenologists of the day found the idea insulting, even absurd. Some called it a "romance," a fantasy. One critic described the proposed relationship as a kind of enslavement, with the fungus as master and the alga as captive, and he found the notion so distasteful that it seemed to count against the hypothesis on aesthetic grounds. The idea that a respected category of living thing might be a kind of arrangement rather than a being struck people as a category error committed by nature itself.

Among those who took the dual hypothesis seriously was a young woman in London who spent her days drawing fungi with extraordinary precision. She germinated spores, observed them under the microscope, and developed her own ideas about how lichens worked. Her paper on the germination of fungal spores was read before the Linnean Society in 1897, though not by her, since women were not permitted to attend. Her name was Beatrix Potter. A few years later she turned her attention to rabbits in waistcoats, and the scientific world lost track of her. It is one of those counterfactual histories that is fun to imagine. She could draw a hedgehog in a bonnet, but she could also see that the orange smudge on a garden wall was two lives braided into one.

---

Out of the fight over lichens came a word. In 1877, the German botanist Albert Bernhard Frank, thinking about exactly this problem, needed a neutral term for organisms living together, one that didn't prejudge whether the arrangement was parasitism, slavery, or friendship. He used a word that became, shortly afterward in the hands of Anton de Bary, "symbiosis." It's worth sitting with that for a moment. The concept that now underpins so much of biology, including the mitochondria in our cells, the bacteria in our guts, the fungi threaded through the roots of nearly every plant, the corals and their algae, had one of its earliest homes in the study of lichens. The gold crust on the gravestone gave us a way to think about ourselves.

Because we are, it turns out, also arrangements. The mitochondria that power your cells were once free-living bacteria, taken in by some ancestral cell perhaps two billion years ago, and never let go. They still have their own DNA. They still divide on their own schedule. You are, in a quite literal sense, a lichen of sorts: a long-settled negotiation between lineages that once lived apart. The line between "an organism" and "a partnership" is not as bright as it looks.

---

The story did not end with Schwendener, either. In 2016, a team led by Toby Spribille published a finding that reopened the whole question. Examining some common lichens, they discovered that many of them contained a third partner: a yeast, a single-celled fungus from an entirely different lineage, embedded in the outer layer of the lichen body. It had been there all along, for perhaps millions of years, hidden in plain sight in organisms that had been studied for more than a century. In some cases, the presence and abundance of this yeast seemed to correlate with differences between lichens that had been classified as separate species.

So a lichen is not a duet. It may be a trio, or a small ensemble, or, as some researchers have begun to suggest, a whole community: bacteria, multiple fungi, algae, all participating in some way. The more closely you look, the less the lichen resembles a thing and the more it resembles an ecosystem that has decided to wear a single coat.

I find this deeply satisfying, and also a little dizzying. It means that one of the most basic questions in biology, "what is an individual?", does not have a clean answer. We tend to assume that nature comes pre-divided into units, that there are things and then there are relationships between things. Lichens suggest that sometimes the relationship comes first, and the "thing" is simply what a durable relationship looks like from the outside.

---

Then there is the slowness.

Some lichens grow fast, by lichen standards, a few millimeters or even a centimeter or so in a year. But many of the crustose lichens, the ones that look painted onto rock, grow almost unimaginably slowly. The map lichen, *Rhizocarpon geographicum*, named for its patchwork of yellow-green territories bordered by black lines like countries on an atlas, can grow at rates measured in fractions of a millimeter per year, and in harsh Arctic conditions slower still. Some individual lichens are thought to be many centuries old, and estimates for the oldest run into the thousands of years.

This slowness has been turned into a tool. Geologists use a technique called lichenometry to date surfaces, such as the rocks left behind by retreating glaciers or the debris of old rockfalls. If you know roughly how fast a given species grows in a given climate, you can measure the largest lichen on a boulder and estimate how long that boulder has been exposed to the sky. The lichen becomes a clock. It is a crude one, with plenty of uncertainty, but it is a clock made of patience.

Think about what it means to be that kind of living thing. A lichen on an alpine boulder might spend most of the year dried out, frozen, or buried under snow, doing essentially nothing. Lichens are masters of what biologists call poikilohydry: they don't regulate their water content. When it's dry, they dry out completely and go dormant. When it rains, or fog rolls in, or dew forms, they soak it up within minutes and resume photosynthesis as though nothing happened. They live in brief bursts, separated by long pauses that would kill almost any other organism.

This makes them astonishingly hardy. In experiments conducted by the European Space Agency, samples of certain lichens were exposed to the conditions of outer space, including vacuum, extreme cold, and intense ultraviolet and cosmic radiation, for days at a time on the outside of orbiting spacecraft. When they were returned to Earth and rehydrated, many of them resumed photosynthesis. They had, in their own way, simply waited it out.

There is something in this that feels almost like a philosophy. We tend to measure life by activity: growth, motion, output. The lichen measures life by persistence. It is not trying to get anywhere. It is trying to still be there when the rain comes back.

---

Lichens are also, quietly, among the great pioneers. When a volcano creates new land, or a glacier retreats and leaves behind bare rock, lichens are often among the first living things to colonize it. They cling to surfaces where nothing else can gain purchase. Over long periods, the acids they produce and the physical expansion and contraction of their bodies as they wet and dry help to break down rock. Their dead tissue accumulates. Dust gets trapped. Eventually, in the tiny crevices they have helped to make, there is enough grit and organic matter for mosses to take hold, and then grasses, and then, over centuries, perhaps forests.

It's humbling to consider that a great deal of the soil we depend on began, at some point, with something like a lichen patiently dissolving stone. The first gardeners of barren ground were not plants but partnerships.

---

They are also sensitive in a way that makes them uncannily useful to us. Many lichens absorb nearly everything from the air and rain, since they have no roots and no protective waxy cuticle like a leaf. They take in water and nutrients across their entire surface, and along with those, pollutants. Sulfur dioxide, in particular, is devastating to many species.

During the Industrial Revolution in Britain, lichens vanished from the trees and walls of industrial cities. Bark that had once been mottled pale with lichen turned dark with soot and bare. This change is tied to one of the most famous stories in evolutionary biology: the peppered moth, whose pale form had been camouflaged against lichen-covered bark, and whose dark form became more common as the lichens disappeared and the trees darkened. Then, as clean air legislation took effect in the twentieth century, the lichens began to return, and the pale moths with them.

Today, lichens are used as biomonitors. Their presence, absence, and diversity on trees and stones can tell you something about the air quality of a place over years, not just on the day you happen to measure it. A city park with a rich variety of leafy and shrubby lichens is breathing relatively clean air. A place with only a few tolerant crusts is telling you something else.

The same absorbent quality made lichens a channel for something much darker. After the Chernobyl disaster in 1986, radioactive fallout drifted across Scandinavia. Lichens, especially the "reindeer lichens" that carpet the northern tundra and form a major winter food source for reindeer, absorbed radioactive caesium from the fallout. Reindeer ate the lichen. The Sámi herders who depended on the reindeer found that meat from many animals was contaminated, sometimes far beyond safe limits. Because lichens grow so slowly and retain what they absorb for so long, the effects lingered for years. A disaster in Ukraine traveled, through the patient metabolism of a tundra lichen, into the livelihoods of people a thousand miles away.

It's a reminder that the same qualities that make lichens admirable, namely their patience, their openness, and their long memory, also make them vulnerable to what we do. They hold on to things.

---

And they are beautiful, once you start looking. That's the part that tends to surprise people. At a glance, lichens are just smudges and crusts, the visual equivalent of background noise. But a hand lens changes everything. Suddenly the grey patch on a fence post becomes a landscape of tiny cups, like miniature golf tees or trumpets, some of them rimmed with red. The pale crust on a boulder turns out to be dotted with black discs, the fruiting bodies of the fungal partner. The "old man's beard" hanging from a conifer resolves into a delicate, branching network, strands with a stretchy central cord you can find if you pull one gently apart.

People have used lichens for dyes for centuries: purples, rusts, yellows, and browns. The traditional orange-brown of some Harris Tweed was associated with lichen dyes, and litmus, the pH indicator every student meets in a chemistry lab, was originally derived from lichens. Some lichens have been eaten in times of famine, after careful preparation. Some have been used in perfumes. Oakmoss, a lichen despite its name, has long been a component of fragrances. The humble crust turns out to have been woven into human life in countless small ways.

---

I keep coming back to that gravestone, though.

The usual story we tell about such a stone is a story about loss. The name fades; the dates blur; the person recedes into anonymity. And that is true, as far as it goes. But what is growing over the name is not nothing. It is a relationship that has persisted for centuries, perhaps longer than the family line of the person buried there. It is a small, slow civilization of fungus and alga and yeast and bacteria, cooperating through drought and frost and pollution, patiently turning stone into the beginnings of soil.

I don't want to be too sentimental about it. Lichens are not moral exemplars. The relationship between the partners is not necessarily friendly. There is ongoing debate about how much the photosynthetic partner benefits, and some have argued the fungus is more farmer than friend. Nature does not arrange itself into parables for our convenience.

But I think the lichen does offer at least one lesson that is hard to argue with. It shows that the boundaries we draw around individuals are, to some extent, conveniences. What we call a "being" may be a long-standing agreement between many beings. What we call "identity" may be the shape a relationship takes when it lasts long enough. And what we call "life" may be less about constant motion and more about the capacity to wait, to endure, and to begin again the moment the rain returns.

When I think about the enormous argument that erupted in the nineteenth century, respectable scientists insisting that a lichen *must* be a single thing, because the alternative was too strange, too romantic, too undignified, I feel a certain tenderness toward them. They were defending a world that was neatly divided. The lichen offered them a world that was tangled, collaborative, and uncertain about its own edges. It took decades for the tangled world to win.

It is still winning, quietly, on walls and roofs and tree trunks and gravestones everywhere. It is not in a hurry. It never has been. It grows, in some places, by less than a millimeter a year, and it has already outlasted most of the people who argued about it.

The next time you pass an old stone gone gold and grey, it might be worth stopping for a moment. What you're looking at is not simply the past being erased. It's a very old conversation, still going on, one that has been making the world a little more habitable, one slow sentence at a time.
